passage: Try to tickle yourself, and you will notice that nothing happens. Even if you touch exactly the same spot with exactly the same movement, the sensation that makes you laugh when someone else does it is almost {1|absent}. Scientists explain this by looking at the cerebellum, a part of the brain that helps to control movement. When you decide to move your hand, the cerebellum predicts the touch that will result and sends a message to the parts of the brain that handle sensation. The message tells them to turn down their response, because the touch is expected. In other words, the brain quietly cancels out the feelings that we cause ourselves. A tickle from another person, by contrast, is a surprise, and nothing {2|reduces} the response, so the skin feels every detail. Experiments support this idea. In one study, volunteers used a robot arm to touch their own palms. When the robot copied their movements at once, the touch felt {3|more} ticklish than when a delay was added. The longer the delay, the more ticklish the touch became, because the brain's prediction no longer matched what was felt. This ability to predict our own actions is useful in daily life. It {4|allows} us to ignore the constant feeling of our clothes and our own breathing, and to focus on unexpected events that might matter, such as a stranger's hand on our shoulder. In this sense, the skill is {5|essential} for telling the difference between ourselves and the world around us.

부위별 간지럼의 차이는 나오지 않습니다.
